column2: Hrothgar's great mead-hall in Denmark, the center of feasting and gift-giving that Grendel attacks for twelve years.

Hrothgar's queen, a gracious peace-weaver who passes the mead-cup and asks Beowulf to be kind to her sons.
A Danish warrior, jealous of Beowulf, who mocks him over the swimming match with Breca and later lends him the sword Hrunting.

column1: 09. Why Beowulf uses no weapon on Grendel
column2: Grendel uses no weapon himself, and Grendel was protected by a charm so that no sword could harm him.
In her underwater lair Unferth's sword Hrunting fails, so Beowulf kills her with an ancient giant's sword he finds on the wall.

column1: 11. What happens to the giant sword
column2: After Beowulf cuts off dead Grendel's head, the blade melts like an icicle in the monster's hot blood, leaving only the hilt.

column1: 12. What Beowulf brings back from the mere
column2: Only Grendel's head and the jeweled hilt of the giant sword, though he saw treasure everywhere.
As an old king Beowulf fights the dragon with his sword Naegling, which snaps, and with Wiglaf's help finishes it with his knife but is fatally bitten.

column1: 14. What Beowulf gets from the dragon fight
column2: Wiglaf brings out some of the hoard so the dying king can see it, but the treasure is buried with Beowulf, so he brings nothing home.

column1: 15. Hrothgar's advice before Beowulf goes home
column2: His "sermon": beware of pride, remember that strength and life fade, share your treasure, and choose eternal rewards.
Each man must die, so he should "win glory before death," because fame is a warrior's best memorial; it is better to avenge than to mourn.
A runaway slave steals a jeweled cup from the dragon's hoard, and the angry dragon burns the Geats' land, including Beowulf's hall.

column1: 18. Who stands by Beowulf against the dragon
column2: Only Wiglaf, who remembers the gifts Beowulf gave him and says he would rather burn beside his lord.

column1: 19. Who does not stand by Beowulf
column2: His ten other hand-picked warriors flee into the woods, and Wiglaf condemns them to lose their lands and honor.
The Geats burn him on a pyre hung with helmets and shields, build a barrow on the headland, bury the treasure with him, and twelve warriors ride around it praising him.

column1: 21. What the Geats fear after Beowulf dies
column2: With their king dead, they expect enemies such as the Swedes to attack, and a Geat woman's lament foretells invasion, slaughter, and slavery.
The poem praises pagan heroic ideals of strength, loyalty, gifts, and fame, while a Christian narrator credits God and warns, through Hrothgar, against pride.
Young Beowulf wins glory for himself, while old King Beowulf must protect a whole people, and his death leaves them exposed.
She seeks revenge for her son, following the same blood-feud code the human warriors live by.
